jwt.verify accepts the 'none' algorithm (algorithms: ['HS256', 'none']). An attacker can forge a token with header {"alg":"none"} and no signature, supplying arbitrary userId/role claims (e.g. role:'admin'). The /dashboard/cost-allocation route has no authenticate middleware and trusts this cookie-based claim, granting admin-scoped data.

extra.message: reportPartnerDeliveryStatus reflects the request Origin header directly into Access-Control-Allow-Origin for any origin, bypassing the approved-partner allow-list (enforced only in the -v2 variant). This is an overly permissive CORS configuration.

JWT signing/verification falls back to a hardcoded secret 'dev-secret-change-in-production' when JWT_SECRET is not set (also at auth.ts:30, audit.ts:57, dashboard.ts:41). If the env var is unset, anyone can forge valid tokens.
Database password falls back to a hardcoded default 'postgres' when DB_PASSWORD is not set. Combined with synchronize:true this is a weak default credential for the production database.

The case-file seal encryption key falls back to the hardcoded secret 'dev-case-file-seal-secret' when CASE_FILE_SEAL_SECRET is not set, allowing anyone who knows this default to decrypt or forge sealed case-file packets.

unsealCaseFilePacket uses unauthenticated AES-256-CBC and deliberately distinguishes padding errors (INVALID_PADDING) from other failures; the open-sealed-packet route surfaces this difference to callers, creating a padding-oracle enabling ciphertext manipulation.
